topics.name: Phases of mitosis
topics.summary: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, and what happens to the chromosomes in each.

topics.name: Cytokinesis
topics.summary: The division of the cytoplasm that follows mitosis.

topics.name: Chromosome number
topics.summary: Daughter cells are genetically identical, with the same number of chromosomes.

items.prompt: In your own words: why do cells divide by mitosis?
items.answer: To grow, to replace old or damaged cells and help healing, and in single-celled organisms to reproduce, making two genetically identical cells.
items.explanation: Mitosis makes more cells that are copies of the parent, which is what growth and repair need.

items.prompt: What does "genetically identical daughter cells" mean?
items.answer: Both new cells have the same DNA as the parent cell.
items.explanation: Identical means the DNA was copied and split equally, so nothing is lost or added.

items.prompt: What happens to the nuclear envelope in prophase?
items.answer: It breaks down, while the chromosomes condense and become visible.
items.explanation: Prophase gets the chromosomes ready: they condense and the envelope around the nucleus breaks down.

items.answer: The sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell, and each chromatid becomes a separate chromosome.

items.prompt: How is cytokinesis different from mitosis?
items.answer: Mitosis copies the DNA and separates it into two new nuclei; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, giving two separate daughter cells.
items.explanation: One splits the nucleus, the other splits the rest of the cell.

keyIdeas.label: Mitosis separates the DNA into two nuclei

items.prompt: A drug stops spindle fibres from attaching to the centromeres. Which phase can't happen, and why?
items.answer: Anaphase: the spindle fibres attached to the centromeres are what pull the sister chromatids apart, so without them the chromatids are never separated.
items.explanation: Metaphase is where the fibres attach; anaphase is where they pull.

keyIdeas.label: Spindle fibres pull the chromatids apart

items.prompt: In which phase do chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell?
items.explanation: In metaphase the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell, with spindle fibres attached to the centromeres.

choices.why: In prophase the chromosomes condense; they haven't lined up yet.
Chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase.
In anaphase the chromatids are already being pulled apart.
In telophase new nuclear envelopes form.

items.prompt: Which of these is not a job of mitosis?
What do spindle fibres attach to in metaphase?
items.explanation: Spindle fibres attach to the centromeres, ready to pull the chromatids apart.

items.prompt: Which phase comes right before cytokinesis?
items.explanation: Telophase is the last phase of mitosis; cytokinesis follows it.
Telophase: the nuclear envelopes form again around each set of chromosomes.

cloze.text: During {{telophase}}, new nuclear envelopes form around each set of chromosomes.

items.explanation: Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells.

cloze.text: Mitosis produces two genetically {{identical}} daughter cells.

items.explanation: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm.

cloze.text: {{Cytokinesis}} is the division of the cytoplasm.

items.prompt: Label the four phases of mitosis.
items.explanation: Left to right: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

items.answer: The division of the cytoplasm, producing two separate daughter cells. It happens right after mitosis.
Chromosomes condense and become visible, and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
